title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align within a Generative AI–enhanced feedback system for higher education, and how differences across these human evaluation sources can inform better AI-generated feedback. The central problem is that many GenAI feedback systems aggregate teacher and peer input as if all sources were equally reliable, while often ignoring self-assessment, despite known differences in bias, consistency, and evaluative perspective.

The study was conducted within the AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback) system, which supports rubric-based assessment of engineering students’ oral presentations and is linked to the GePeTo generative AI model for feedback generation. The researchers analyzed 46 complete evaluation sets consisting of teacher rubric scores, two peer assessments, one self-assessment, and the teacher’s independent overall grade. Using statistical analyses of agreement, correlation, and mean differences, the study examined how closely these sources matched and where systematic scoring biases appeared. Based on these findings, the authors propose an enhanced GenAI design that uses weighted integration of teacher, peer, and self inputs, along with bias detection and context-aware feedback generation.

Participants were 46 final-year undergraduate engineering students in a compulsory oral communication course at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid in Spain. Presentations were delivered face-to-face in class, with two randomly assigned peers and the course teacher evaluating each presentation in real time using the same validated rubric; students later completed self-assessments while watching recordings of their presentations. The course context was authentic and classroom-embedded, focused on oral presentation skills in engineering education.

The main conclusions are that peer, self, and teacher assessments showed moderate to substantial agreement overall, and all rubric-based scores were significantly correlated with the teacher’s overall grade, with teacher scores aligning most strongly and self-assessments the least. Students tended to rate themselves and peers slightly more leniently than the teacher did, while the teacher’s detailed rubric scores were lower than her own holistic overall grades. The authors argue that these systematic differences should not be ignored in AI feedback systems; instead, they should be modeled explicitly so GenAI can produce more pedagogically valid, transparent, and human-centered feedback.

identified_tools.name: AICoFe
identified_tools.description: An AI-based Collaborative Feedback system developed at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid that integrates teacher, peer, and self-assessments using a rubric and uses a generative AI model to produce personalized feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the assessment and feedback platform for engineering students' oral presentations, collecting teacher, peer, and self-evaluations and informing an enhanced GenAI-based feedback design.

findings.finding_summary: Across 46 full evaluation sets of engineering students’ oral presentations, agreement among teacher, peer, and self-assessments in AICoFe was moderate to substantial by Gwet’s AC2, despite weak weighted Cohen’s kappa values. Pairwise AC2 ranged from 0.58 to 0.63, exact agreement ranged from 0.43 to 0.53, Kendall’s W was 0.51 for teacher and peers and 0.46 when self-assessment was included, indicating meaningful but imperfect evaluator consistency.
findings.measure: Inter-rater agreement on rubric-based oral presentation scores (weighted Cohen’s kappa, Gwet’s AC2, exact agreement, Kendall’s W)

findings.finding_summary: Rubric-based scores collected through AICoFe were significantly associated with the teacher’s independently assigned overall grade for oral presentations. Correlations were strongest for the teacher rubric mean (r=0.88, ρ=0.89), followed by the mean rubric score across all evaluators (r=0.85, ρ=0.86), peers rubric mean (r=0.69, ρ=0.68), and self-assessment rubric mean (r=0.59, ρ=0.67), with all reported as p<0.001.
findings.measure: Correlation between rubric-based scores and teacher’s overall grade for oral presentations

findings.finding_summary: Bias analyses within AICoFe showed systematic scoring differences across evaluator sources. The teacher’s rubric scores were significantly lower than peers’ scores (mean difference -0.49, p=0.008) and lower than the teacher’s own overall grade (mean difference -0.37, p<0.001), while self-assessments were significantly higher than teacher rubric scores (mean difference +0.36, p=0.037); other comparisons were not statistically significant.
findings.measure: Mean score differences across teacher, peer, self, and overall grade sources on a 0–10 scale

identified_tools.name: GePeTo
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-based personalized guidance and feedback model integrated within AICoFe to generate personalized feedback from rubric-based evaluation data.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as the generative model within AICoFe and proposed for enhancement through weighted evaluator input aggregation, bias detection, and context-aware feedback generation; not directly empirically evaluated for outcome impact in this paper.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study, but it is correlational/descriptive rather than an RCT or strong quasi-experiment. The paper analyzes evaluator agreement, correlations, and bias in one higher-education course with n=46.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports agreement and correlation metrics and proposes design improvements, but it does not test causal impact of the AI-generated feedback on student learning outcomes. As a result, impact is suggestive but unclear.
